justification_text:
The point estimates for each horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are set at the same value of 52.72 because they represent the best central forecast based on the information available at the time the projection was made. This estimate likely reflects a current trend or equilibrium value derived from a model that accounts for the underlying drivers of the variable being forecasted. Over these short-to-medium time horizons, we assume no significant shifts in these drivers, keeping the baseline estimate unchanged.

The widths of the confidence intervals grow as the time horizon extends because uncertainty accumulates over time. For a 1-day forecast, the sources of uncertainty are quite limited, so the 90% confidence interval is relatively tight (51.95 to 53.49). Over the course of a week or a month, however, more factors can come into play, such as new data, unexpected developments, or compounding noise in the system being modeled. These additional layers of uncertainty result in wider confidence intervals at 1 week (50.8 to 54.64) and 1 month (48.9 to 56.54), reflecting the growing difficulty of making precise predictions as the forecast horizon lengthens.

Certain risks or events could materially change the outcome, potentially causing it to fall outside the stated confidence intervals. For example, abrupt shocks such as economic crises, geopolitical events, regulatory changes, or extreme weather events could disrupt the normal patterns underlying this forecast. Even more minor, unexpected developments in the variable's key drivers could skew outcomes toward the edges of, or even beyond, the stated ranges. These intervals assume a degree of "business-as-usual," so any significant deviation from that expectation could push the actual results outside the model's predicted boundaries.
